steps: Configure the monitoring portfolio in Brand Visibility from your approved prompt plan, with the agreed markets, languages and competitors, and confirm each pilot user can open the workspace.
Agree the delivery-network setup and crawler access for each site in week one, set a date for the log-forwarding job, and register CDN log forwarding in Brand Visibility.
Confirm the CDN logs arrive once the log-forwarding job is active, with agentic and referral traffic flowing into Brand Visibility.
Record the baseline for the agreed prompts and competitors, with the engines, market and measurement dates, and list the first opportunities in priority order.
deliverables: Configured monitoring portfolio in Brand Visibility
CDN log forwarding with agentic and referral traffic
asks: Your approved prompt plan, the competitors to track and the names of the pilot users
A CDN contact who can set up the log-forwarding job in your CDN console
Crawler access for Adobe's scanner (Spacecat/1.0) and the AI crawlers in robots.txt and bot rules
risk: A CDN log-forwarding job that runs late: we set its date in week one and start the prompt work before it is live.
outcome: Brand Visibility tracks how your brand appears in AI-generated answers against a recorded baseline, with agentic and referral traffic arriving from your CDN logs.

steps: Decide each month which prompts to keep, add or retire, and log every change, keeping the stable trend cohort apart from new discovery prompts.
Read the visibility and citation trends against your named peers, and the Impact Measurement Engine's results for deployment pilots, noting sampling limits.
Prioritize the actions for the month with an owner for each, and route site changes to Sites Optimizer's monthly fixes where they are included, or to your web team.
Hold the monthly review with your team on the agreed business measures, keeping visibility, AI-agent activity and AI-referred visits and conversions as separate measures.
deliverables: Visibility and citation trends against named peers
asks: Access to your existing analytics reports for AI-referred visits and conversions
The people who attend the monthly review and own its actions
risk: Reading a change in the prompt set as a change in results: we keep a stable trend cohort and claim business impact only from a tested comparison.
outcome: Each month your team sees what changed, what it means and which actions come first, with an owner and a next decision for each.

steps: Pick the month's pages from the agreed priorities and write a brief for each, with the question it answers and the approved facts it uses.
Refresh the agreed existing pages and write the new answer page in your existing templates, with clear answers, supporting evidence, internal links and metadata.
Run the agreed review rounds with your reviewers for factual accuracy and relevance, and publish the approved pages.
Log each page change once, tagged search, AI or both, and check the published pages against their briefs.
deliverables: Published page refreshes and new answer page
Page change log tagged search, AI or both
asks: Source facts and reviewers who approve accuracy and relevance
Publishing access and your existing page templates
risk: Facts that drift from your approved sources: every page is written from the brief's approved facts and goes through your review rounds before it is published.
outcome: Each month, more of your pages give clear, sourced answers that people and every search engine see, with each change logged.

steps: Prioritize each month the publications, review roundups, directories and other independent sources that AI answers cite for the agreed prompts.
Create evidence-based pitch assets from the facts you supply, and have your reviewers approve every claim before any outreach.
Complete the authorized outreach actions and sourced correction requests, proposing any Wikipedia change on the article's talk page with the paid-contribution disclosure Wikipedia requires.
Record each action, its outcome and any mentions, links or citations observed, with publisher decisions kept separate in the outreach record.
deliverables: Outreach record with observed mentions and citations
asks: Credible evidence, and reviewers who approve every claim before outreach
Explicit authorization for the outreach actions taken on your behalf
risk: Outreach that reads as paid or undisclosed: you approve every claim, and we propose Wikipedia changes on the talk page with the required disclosure.
outcome: Independent sources that AI answers cite receive accurate, evidence-based material about your brand, with every action and its outcome on record.

steps: Review Brand Visibility Referral Traffic and your conversion data to choose the month's landing, product or answer experiences and next-step path.
Write a brief for each change and design it with your current components, destinations and measurement in your existing CMS.
Make the approved changes and run the agreed content, accessibility, consent and event-validation checks before they go live.
Report the observed performance of each change, and claim lift from a change only where an appropriate test supports it.
asks: Access to your CMS and your existing conversion data
Reviewers who approve changes, including any regulated content or offered action
risk: A change that breaks tracking or consent: every change passes the agreed accessibility, consent and event-validation checks before it goes live.
outcome: The agreed experiences and next-step path carry your approved changes, each checked before it goes live, with its observed performance reported.

steps: Agree the hypothesis, the pages, the business measure and the variants or cohorts, and confirm your tracking and traffic can support the test.
Design the measurement plan with matched untreated pages or a staged comparison where feasible, and agree the method with you before launch.
Configure the test in your existing measurement tools, record the setup and QA evidence, and log concurrent changes such as AI model updates, campaigns and competitor moves.
Analyze the results and deliver the readout, explaining the evidence and its limits, saying plainly when a result is inconclusive, and recommending next steps.
asks: Access to your analytics or testing tools, with stable tracking on the agreed pages
An owner who approves the test method before launch
risk: Results confused by other changes: we use matched untreated pages or a staged comparison where feasible and log AI model updates, campaigns and competitor moves.
outcome: You have a tested answer, conclusive or not, on whether the agreed optimization moved the agreed business measure, with its evidence and limits stated.

steps: Review each month the Reddit and community threads that AI answers cite for the agreed prompts, with each community's participation rules, and list the opportunities.
Draft useful, evidence-based answers from your approved facts and expertise, with source references, for your approval.
Submit approved answers where the community permits it, through your authorized accounts with brand-affiliation disclosure, and record each attempt, moderation decision and response.
deliverables: Approved answer drafts with source references
asks: Approved facts and an expert who can review each answer
Authorized accounts, and explicit approval for each submission
risk: A contribution that breaks a community's rules: we read each community's current rules first and submit only approved, disclosed answers through authorized accounts.
outcome: You have approved, disclosed answers for the threads AI answers cite, submitted where each community allows them, with every attempt and moderation decision on record.

steps: Map each month the videos that appear in AI answers to the tracked prompts against your priority customer questions, using Brand Visibility's cited-video analysis.
Improve each agreed video's title, description, chapter markers, captions and destination links from your approved facts, for your reviewers to approve.
Publish the approved updates in your existing YouTube channel, run the agreed quality checks, and record the before and after channel measures.
deliverables: Publishing record with before and after channel measures
asks: Access to your YouTube channel and the videos to update
Approved source facts and reviewers who check factual accuracy
risk: A month when AI answers cite none of your videos: we agree with you whether that month's time goes to other off-site work.
outcome: Your cited videos answer your priority customer questions in their titles, descriptions, chapters and captions, with approved facts and the right destination links.

steps: Agree the priority customer question and the production format, then write the script and storyboard from your approved facts.
Make a simple edit from the approved footage and brand assets you provide, and add captions, title, description and destination links.
Run the agreed review rounds with your reviewers for factual accuracy, and check the video, captions, metadata and links against the selected checks.
Upload the final video to your channel once you authorize it, and record the publishing details.
deliverables: Final answer video with caption file
asks: Usable footage, brand assets and the rights to use them
Approved facts, reviewers and access to your YouTube channel
risk: Footage that cannot answer the question well: we agree the question and storyboard against your available footage before editing begins.
outcome: You have a short, captioned video that answers a priority customer question, approved by your reviewers and published on your channel.

steps: Agree with your team which pages and assets to analyze, and the key performance indicators your content is measured against.
Confirm Web SDK or Mobile SDK data collection on the agreed sites and apps, and record any gaps in a readiness checklist.
Allow-list the user agent and IP address of the featurization service used in Content Analytics, with your security team.
Set the CJA and data collection permissions for the people who will configure and use Content Analytics.
deliverables: Readiness checklist with gaps and owners
Allow-list record for the featurization service
CJA and data collection permission settings
Agreed list of pages and assets
asks: A security or network contact who can allow-list the featurization service
An administrator who can grant CJA and data collection permissions
risk: A prerequisite found missing during configuration: we confirm data collection, the allow-list and permissions on a readiness checklist before setup starts.
outcome: Your sites and apps are ready for Content Analytics, with data collection confirmed, the featurization service allow-listed, permissions set and the pages and assets agreed.

steps: Run Adobe's guided configuration wizard for Content Analytics, choosing the sandbox, connection and data views with your team.
Set the web and mobile channels and experience capture, and write exclusion rules that keep personal data out of what is collected.
Implement the configuration, and review it with your team against the agreed pages, channels and exclusion rules before anything is published.
Publish the Tags property with your sign-off, which deploys the configuration and starts data collection, then check that impressions and interactions are recorded.
deliverables: Content Analytics configuration in the agreed sandbox
Published Tags property and first-data check
asks: A decision on the sandbox, data views and channels to configure
Sign-off to publish the Tags property, and a privacy reviewer for exclusion rules
risk: Personal data collected by mistake: we agree the exclusion rules with your privacy reviewer before the Tags property is published, and check the first data collected.
outcome: Content Analytics is deployed and collecting data on your agreed web and mobile channels, with personal data kept out by exclusion rules.

steps: Agree with your web team the analyzed pages where page experiences are captured, and when a page change counts as a new version.
Add the adobe.getContentExperienceVersion function to those pages, so each page change is recorded as a new experience.
Test on a sample page by publishing a change and checking that it is collected as a new experience.
deliverables: Versioning on the agreed analyzed pages
Test record for a sample page change
asks: A web developer who can add the function to your page templates
A list of the analyzed pages and how often they change
risk: Page changes that are not collected as new experiences: we add versioning to each analyzed page where experiences are captured and test a change before sign-off.
outcome: When an analyzed page changes, the change is recorded as a new experience, so your content results stay tied to the right version.

steps: Agree with your paid media team the Google Ads and Meta Ads accounts in scope, and the tracking keys your campaigns use.
Connect Google Ads and Meta Ads through Experience Platform's source connectors, and enable the paid media channel on their datasets.
Map the tracking keys between your experience event data and paid media data, and set up the reporting configuration that links ad content to site conversions.
Check a sample of campaigns end to end, from ad to site conversion, and record the mapping in a tracking-key sheet.
deliverables: Google Ads and Meta Ads source connections
Paid media channel on their datasets
Tracking-key mapping sheet and test results
asks: Access to your Google Ads and Meta Ads accounts so we can connect them
Your paid media team's tracking-key conventions for each campaign
risk: Ad data that does not match site visits: we agree the tracking keys first and test a sample of campaigns from ad to conversion before sign-off.
outcome: Content from your Google Ads and Meta Ads campaigns links to site conversions, so your team can see which ad content leads to them.

steps: Set up the Content Analytics Workspace template, so your team starts from a pre-populated project with content insights.
Build the core freeform reports with thumbnails and previews for the agreed questions, such as which assets receive impressions and where.
Share the projects with each team, whose access runs through the data views configured for Content Analytics.
Train your analysts and content teams to read attribute insights, such as the average click through rate for assets with certain attributes, using your own content.
deliverables: Content Analytics Workspace project from the template
Core freeform reports with thumbnails and previews
asks: The names and roles of the analysts and content team members to train
The questions each team most needs its content reports to answer
risk: Reports that teams do not use: we build the core reports around each team's own questions and train on your own content.
outcome: Your analysts and content teams see which assets and attributes drive engagement, from shared Content Analytics projects in Customer Journey Analytics.

steps: Review each month which assets and attributes drive engagement and conversion on your web and mobile properties.
Flag the assets that are underused or overused, with the evidence behind each flag.
Feed the findings into your content plan with your content leads, as actions with an owner and a date.
deliverables: Actions added to your content plan
asks: A content lead who joins the monthly review and owns the content plan
risk: Findings that never reach the content plan: we turn each one into an action with an owner and a date, agreed with your content lead.
outcome: Each month your content plan reflects which assets and attributes drive engagement and conversion, and which assets are underused or overused.

steps: Create a derived field on AI referring domains in the CJA data view, to find AI-referred visitors in your existing web data.
Define the agreed audiences from AI-referred visits and their outcomes, after agreeing the Person ID that CJA sends as each member's primary identity.
Publish the audiences to Real-Time Customer Profile and check that they populate with the agreed definitions.
Agree with each channel owner how the audience is used in your existing channels, covering identity, consent and intended use, in an activation plan with owners.
deliverables: Audiences published to Real-Time Customer Profile
asks: A CJA administrator who also has Experience Platform's Manage Profiles permission
Channel owners who confirm identity, consent and intended use for each audience
risk: An audience used beyond what consent allows: each channel owner confirms identity, consent and intended use in the activation plan before the audience is used.
outcome: Audiences of AI-referred visitors, defined by their outcomes, sit in Real-Time Customer Profile, ready for your existing channels under an agreed activation plan.

steps: Agree with your data team the channels CJA will report on, and the source system behind each one, in a source inventory.
Design the XDM schemas that standardize your customer experience data, with the fields each channel needs and a customer ID they share.
Create the datasets in Experience Platform and set up ingestion for each agreed channel, starting with a sample load.
Check each dataset against its source for record counts and field values on an agreed day, and record the results.
deliverables: Source inventory for the agreed channels
XDM schemas and datasets in Experience Platform
asks: A data team contact for each source system, with access to sample data
The list of channels and source systems CJA will report on
risk: Channel data that cannot be combined later: we agree the shared customer ID in the schema design, before any dataset is loaded.
outcome: Data from your agreed channels sits in Experience Platform, standardized in XDM schemas and ready for Customer Journey Analytics to report across channels.

steps: Agree the person ID for each dataset with your data team, and record it in a connection plan with each dataset's owner.
Create the connection that brings your datasets from Adobe Experience Platform into Workspace, with the agreed person ID for each.
Configure field-based or graph-based stitching on eligible event datasets where needed, and check the stitched results on a sample of records.
Build the data views with your agreed components and settings, and check the main metrics against your current reports.
deliverables: Connection plan with person IDs and owners
Data views with agreed components and settings
asks: A data team contact who can agree the person ID for each dataset
The components and settings your teams need in each data view
risk: Wrong person IDs that split or merge people: we agree the ID for each dataset first and check stitched results on a sample before building data views.
outcome: Your datasets reach Workspace through the connection, joined on the right person ID, with data views your teams can report from.

steps: Plan the upgrade path with your analytics team: inventory current reports, projects, components, reporting API use and exports, and agree what moves, changes or retires.
Implement the Experience Platform Web SDK, the preferred data collection method, starting with agreed pages and checking its data against your current reports.
Set up the Analytics source connector alongside the Web SDK, so your history is available in Customer Journey Analytics.
Port your reporting API use and exports to Customer Journey Analytics, and test each one with its owner.
Migrate the agreed projects and components, compare key reports side by side with the old ones, and sign off the cutover with your team.
deliverables: History through the Analytics source connector
Ported reporting API use and exports
asks: Owners for each report, API integration and export that must move
Developer time to implement the Web SDK on your pages
Sign-off from your team on the side-by-side checks before cutover
risk: Reports that no longer match after the upgrade: we compare key reports side by side and sign off each one with its owner before cutover.
outcome: Your reporting runs in Customer Journey Analytics on Web SDK data, with your history, projects, components, API use and exports carried over.

steps: Agree the priority questions with each team, and the KPIs and segments that answer them, in a short project brief.
Build the agreed Analysis Workspace projects on the agreed cross-channel data views, laid out to answer each priority question in turn.
Review each project with its users, check the numbers against an agreed reference report, and make the agreed changes.
Build and share mobile scorecards for the Analytics dashboards app where they are included, and agree who handles app setup for your named executives.
deliverables: Project brief with questions, KPIs and segments
asks: Each team's priority questions, and a person who signs off its project
The named executive users for any mobile scorecards
risk: Projects that answer the wrong questions: we agree each team's priority questions in a brief before building, and review each project with its users.
outcome: Your teams answer their priority questions in shared Analysis Workspace projects, built on agreed cross-channel data views, KPIs and segments.

steps: Map your users by role, from report readers to analysts who build projects, and plan an onboarding path for each.
Train each group in Analysis Workspace on its own tasks, with exercises on your own data.
For users who know Adobe Analytics, cover the key differences, which Adobe advises giving three to six months to learn.
Set up shared components and project templates, so every team starts from agreed metrics and dimensions.
asks: The names and roles of the people to train
Time from each group for the sessions
risk: Users drifting back to old reports: we build the first shared projects with them, so their everyday questions start in Customer Journey Analytics.
outcome: Your analysts and report readers answer their own questions in Customer Journey Analytics, from shared and agreed components.

steps: Agree the priority journeys for the month with your stakeholders, and the question each analysis should answer.
Run flow, fallout and attribution analysis on those journeys in Analysis Workspace, breaking results down by dimension where that explains a change.
Report the findings to your stakeholders in a short monthly readout, with the evidence behind each one.
Recommend next actions with an owner for each, and track last month's actions in the next readout.
deliverables: Monthly journey analysis in Analysis Workspace
asks: Stakeholders who agree the priority journeys and attend the readout
risk: Findings that do not lead to action: each recommendation has an owner, and we report on last month's actions in the next readout.
outcome: Each month your stakeholders see where priority journeys flow, where they fall out and which touchpoints get credit, with next actions agreed.

steps: Agree with your team who needs access to Collaboration and what each person should see and do, in a role plan.
Grant administrator access, and create Permissions roles that include the View Profiles and View Segments permissions audience sourcing needs.
Add the agreed sandboxes and assign the agreed users to their roles.
Confirm each user can open Collaboration and sees what their role allows, and record the results in the role plan.
deliverables: Role plan with users and sandboxes
Access test results for each user
asks: An administrator who can grant access and create Permissions roles
The names of the users and the sandboxes they need
risk: Users who cannot source audiences: we include the View Profiles and View Segments permissions in their roles and test each user's access before handover.
outcome: Each of your users opens Collaboration with a role that decides what they can see and do, including the permissions audience sourcing needs.

steps: Agree the match key strategy with your data and privacy teams, deciding which keys align your audiences across connections.
Define your account's role in Collaboration and create the advertiser or publisher account.
Add your account's name, description, logo and contact email from your approved branding assets.
Configure the agreed match keys that align your audiences across connections, and check them on a test audience.
deliverables: Advertiser or publisher account with branding
asks: Your logo, account description and a contact email for collaborators
Data and privacy leads who agree the match key strategy
risk: Audiences that align poorly with collaborators: we agree the match key strategy with your data and privacy teams before any keys are configured.
outcome: Your Collaboration account carries your branding and role, with the agreed match keys configured to align your audiences across connections.

steps: Agree with your data team which audiences kept outside Experience Platform to bring in, and which cloud data source holds them.
Prepare the audience files to the required schema in Adobe's Audience Specification, with SHA256-hashed identifiers and the required metadata.
Set up the data connection to your Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Snowflake, Azure storage or Databricks Delta Share source.
Load a test file, check it against the specification and the expected record counts, then load the agreed audiences.
deliverables: Audience files to Adobe's Audience Specification
Data connection to your cloud data source
asks: Access to your cloud data source and the audiences it holds
A data team contact who owns the source audiences and their identifiers
risk: Identifiers that leave your systems unhashed: every file uses SHA256-hashed identifiers, and we test one file against the specification before the agreed audiences load.
outcome: Audiences you keep outside Experience Platform reach Collaboration from your cloud data source, as hashed files that follow Adobe's specification.

steps: Agree with your media team which publishers to work with, then find them in the Connect workspace or send them private invitations.
Agree the connection settings with you, such as use cases and credit consumption, then submit them and confirm each connection.
Set up the first project with each collaborator across Discover, Activate and Measure, starting from the audience overlap calculation.
Walk your team through the first project, and record the settings and decisions to reuse for the next collaborator.
deliverables: First project set up with each collaborator
asks: A media lead who chooses the publishers and approves each connection
Decisions on use cases and credit consumption for each connection
risk: Credits spent faster than planned: we agree use cases and credit consumption in each connection's settings with you before submitting them.
outcome: You are connected with the agreed publishers, with settings you approved and a first project ready to discover, activate and measure audiences.

steps: Plan the training by role, from the people who choose audiences to those who report on campaigns, using your own connections.
Train your team to read audience overlap insights, the overlap percentages and number of overlapping identities, and to pick audiences to activate.
Show your team how to add campaign IDs and create campaign summary and attribution reports in the Measure workspace.
Build the first reports with your team on a live campaign, and leave a short guide for each task.
deliverables: First campaign summary and attribution reports
Short task guides for your team
asks: The people to train, and their roles in audience and campaign work
A live campaign and its campaign IDs to use in training
risk: Skills that fade after training: we build the first reports with your team on a live campaign and leave a guide for each task.
outcome: Your team reads audience overlap, picks audiences to activate and reports campaign results in the Measure workspace on its own.

steps: Add or retire audiences each month, and tune their refresh schedules in Collaboration to keep credit use in line with your plan.
Set up projects for the month's new campaigns with the agreed collaborators, using the settings recorded for each connection.
Run overlap and measurement reports with your collaborators, and share a short monthly summary of audiences, credit use and campaign results.
asks: A monthly list of new campaigns and audiences to add or retire
risk: Credit use that runs ahead of plan: we review refresh schedules each month and retire audiences that are no longer in use.
outcome: Your collaborations stay current each month, with the right audiences, refresh schedules that fit your credit plan and reports on every campaign.

steps: Plan your hierarchy of websites, stores and store views with your team, covering brands, markets and languages, in a store structure plan.
Create the websites, stores and store views in the Admin, and set each store's root category and base URL.
Set configuration values at the global, website or store view scope, and choose the base, display and allowed currencies and update their rates.
Create Admin user roles and accounts limited to the websites and stores each team needs, and test each role's access.
deliverables: Websites, stores and store views in the Admin
asks: Decisions on your brands, markets, languages and currencies
The teams that need Admin access, and the stores each one manages
risk: A structure that does not fit how your teams sell: we agree the hierarchy and the scope of each setting in a plan before anything is created.
outcome: Your websites, stores and store views are set up in the Admin, with the right currencies and settings at each scope and access limited by team.

steps: Choose the import method by your catalog's size and how often it changes: manual entry, Admin CSV import, the bulk or asynchronous REST APIs, or the CSV REST API.
Prepare the agreed product data in a mapping sheet, with each source field matched to its catalog attribute and an owner for gaps.
Load a sample batch first by the chosen method, running Check Data and correcting the problems listed for an Admin CSV import.
Load the rest of the agreed product data, review the import history and error file, and check a sample of products on the storefront with your team.
deliverables: Loaded catalog with import history and error review
asks: Your product data export, with an owner who can answer data questions
A merchandiser to check sample products on the storefront
risk: Product data errors that reach the storefront: we load a sample first, correct the problems listed, and check products on the storefront before sign-off.
outcome: Your agreed product data is in Adobe Commerce by the import method that fits your catalog, with errors corrected and the load on record.

steps: Record your approved rules for tax, checkout, shipping and payment in a settings sheet, with your finance and operations teams.
Set the tax classes, rules and rates, guest checkout, and terms and conditions in the Commerce Admin to the agreed rules.
Set the shipping origin, carriers and delivery methods, and the payment methods with their order status, currency and country settings.
Run test transactions in sandbox mode for each payment method before the store goes live, and check tax and delivery on each test order.
deliverables: Tax, checkout, shipping and payment settings
asks: Approved tax, shipping and payment rules from your finance and operations teams
Sandbox access for your payment methods, and your carrier account details
risk: A tax or payment setting that is wrong at launch: every setting traces to an approved rule, and test transactions run in sandbox mode before go-live.
outcome: Your store charges tax, takes payment and offers delivery to your approved rules, tested in sandbox mode before it goes live.

steps: List your fulfillment locations and fulfillment rules with your operations team, and create a source for each location.
Add stocks that map your websites to those sources, and order the sources in each stock.
Assign sources and quantities to products, and check the salable quantity for each stock against your inventory records.
Configure the distance priority algorithm and test sample orders, so shipment recommendations follow your fulfillment rules.
deliverables: Product quantities and salable quantity checks
asks: Your fulfillment locations and the rules for which one ships an order
Current on-hand quantities for each product and location
risk: Shipments recommended from the wrong location: we test sample orders against your fulfillment rules before the store takes live orders.
outcome: Each website sells from the right fulfillment locations, with salable quantities checked and shipment recommendations that follow your fulfillment rules.

steps: Install the Live Search extension with Composer, and connect it with your Commerce API keys.
Sync the catalog data and check the export, matching product counts against your catalog.
Set the searchable and filterable attributes, facets, synonyms and search merchandising rules with your merchandising team.
Test search, category browse and filters on the storefront against an agreed list of common searches, and fix what the tests find.
deliverables: Installed and connected Live Search extension
Search attributes, facets, synonyms and merchandising rules
asks: Your Commerce API keys and access to install the extension
A merchandiser who agrees synonyms, facets and merchandising rules
risk: Shoppers who cannot find products by the words they use: we test an agreed list of common searches and filters on the storefront before launch.
outcome: Live Search replaces the standard search on your store, with facets, synonyms and merchandising rules your team can manage in the Admin.

steps: Agree your B2B rules with your sales and finance teams: company roles, credit limits, pricing by company and purchase order approvals.
Enable company accounts, shared catalogs, B2B quotes and purchase orders in the Admin, and set the default B2B payment and shipping methods and payment on account.
Create the first company accounts with credit limits, and shared catalogs with custom pricing for the agreed companies.
Test company roles, negotiable quotes and purchase order approval rules on the storefront, using test buyers in each agreed role.
deliverables: First company accounts and shared catalogs
Storefront test results for roles, quotes and approvals
asks: Your B2B rules for roles, credit limits, pricing and approvals
The first companies to set up, with their buyers and custom pricing
risk: A buyer who can order beyond their permission: we test each company role and purchase order approval rule on the storefront before buyers are invited.
outcome: Your business buyers order through company accounts with their own roles, credit limits, custom pricing, negotiable quotes and approval rules.

steps: Review the patches your store needs each month, and test them in a staging or development environment before applying them with the Quality Patches Tool.
Plan and test the next Adobe Commerce upgrade with the Upgrade Compatibility Tool, and record what must change before it goes ahead.
Review indexer configuration and site performance, and fix the issues found in an agreed order of priority.
Report each month on the patches applied, the upgrade plan and the issues fixed, with a rollback note for each change.
asks: Access to your staging or development environment and deployment process
A contact who approves each patch and change before it goes live
risk: A patch that breaks the live store: we test every patch in a staging or development environment first, and keep a way to revert it.
outcome: Your store stays patched and ready for its next upgrade, with indexer configuration and site performance reviewed each month.

steps: Map your people by role, department or team, and the Adobe apps and services each group needs, in a profile plan.
Set up the product profiles from the plan, so each profile gives access to the related Adobe apps and services.
Assign users and groups to their profiles, and check a sample of users from each group for the right access.
Name the profile admins who manage assignments, and walk them through adding and removing users.
deliverables: Product profiles with assigned users and groups
asks: A list of your users and groups, by role, department or team
The people who will act as profile admins
risk: People given apps they should not have, or missing ones they need: we agree a profile plan first and check a sample from each group.
outcome: Your people reach the Adobe apps and services their role needs through product profiles, managed day to day by your own profile admins.

steps: Agree the apps, versions, update settings and Marketplace plugins for each group of users with your IT and creative leads.
Build the managed packages for your Windows and macOS devices, controlling which apps and versions are deployed and when updates are applied.
Test each package on sample Windows and macOS devices, checking that the apps, plugins and settings install as agreed.
Hand the tested packages to your IT team for deployment, with a short record of each package's contents and settings.
deliverables: Managed packages for Windows and macOS
asks: Test Windows and macOS devices that match your standard builds
An IT contact who deploys the packages to your devices
risk: A package that fails on your devices: we test each one on sample Windows and macOS devices before your IT team deploys it.
outcome: Your IT team deploys tested packages that give each group the agreed apps, versions, plugins and update settings.

steps: Gather your approved logos, colors, type styles and graphics with your brand team, and agree how the libraries are organized.
Create projects in your business storage, so your organization owns the libraries built in them.
Build the shared libraries in those projects, making brand libraries view-only so designers always have the most up-to-date assets.
Check with a sample of designers that they can pick up the approved elements inside their apps.
asks: Your approved logos, colors, type styles and graphics
A brand owner who approves what goes into each library
risk: Designers using outdated brand elements: brand libraries are view-only and owned by your organization, so the approved version is the one they pick up.
outcome: Your designers pick up approved logos, colors, type styles and graphics inside their apps, from libraries your organization owns.

steps: Agree with your security and legal teams how company content may be shared outside your organization.
Set the asset sharing policy in the Admin Console, restricting sharing features in Creative Cloud and Document Cloud to the agreed rules.
Switch optional services on or off for each product profile, and test sharing and services with a sample user from each profile.
deliverables: Asset sharing policy in the Admin Console
Service settings for each product profile
asks: Security and legal contacts who decide how content may be shared externally
risk: Sensitive content shared with the wrong people: we set the sharing policy to your agreed rules and test it before your teams rely on it.
outcome: Sharing outside your organization follows the rules you agreed, and each product profile has only the optional services you chose.

steps: Agree with your brand team the fonts you are licensed to use, and which users should receive each one.
Accept the Custom fonts offer in the Admin Console and upload the agreed fonts once.
Set which users receive the fonts, and check on a sample device that they sync for use in supported apps.
deliverables: Custom fonts uploaded in the Admin Console
Sync check on a sample device
asks: The font files you are licensed to use, and the users who need them
risk: Fonts shared beyond what your font licenses allow: we upload only the fonts you confirm and assign them to the users you name.
outcome: Your brand fonts sync to the right users' devices for use in supported apps, added once and managed in the Admin Console.

steps: Plan the sessions by team, from designers to reviewers, around the libraries and Adobe products each team uses.
Train your creative teams to use and share libraries in projects with your organization or collaborators, and to work in cloud documents.
Show designers the panels that connect the apps to your other Adobe products, such as the Adobe Asset Link panel for Experience Manager Assets.
Run hands-on exercises with your own files and libraries, and leave short guides your teams can return to.
asks: The names and teams of the people to train
Time from each team for the sessions
risk: Teams that go back to emailing files: we train on their own files and libraries, so shared libraries become part of their daily work.
outcome: Your creative teams share libraries, work in cloud documents and reach your other Adobe products from inside their apps.

steps: Update the managed packages each month for new app versions, and test them before your IT team deploys them.
Add or remove users from your monthly list of joiners, movers and leavers, and assign them to the right product profiles.
Adjust product profiles and their services as needs change, since services are enabled at the profile level, not for individual users.
asks: A monthly list of joiners, movers and leavers from your HR or IT team
risk: Access that outlives a person's role: we process your joiners, movers and leavers list each month and log every change.
outcome: Each month your users have current apps and the right access, with packages, profiles and services kept in step with your teams.

steps: Run workshops with your team to choose bounded workflows for Coworker Chat, with the goal, required inputs and outputs of each.
List the applications and context each workflow draws on, and set the success measures you will judge it by.
Record in the workflow briefs which parts of the work your team, Adobe and we each own, and submit the briefs for your sign-off before configuration begins.
asks: Application owners for each workflow, and your Adobe onboarding contact
Pilot users and leads who can attend the workshops
risk: Workflows too broad to pilot well: we keep each one bounded, with set inputs, outputs and success measures, approved before configuration begins.
outcome: You have approved briefs for bounded Coworker Chat workflows, with inputs, outputs, success measures and a clear split of who does what.

steps: Validate the agreed pilot users and the application context each workflow needs in Coworker Chat, with your administrators.
Review the approved context pack with your team: business terminology, brand guidance and the review responsibilities for each workflow.
Test the agreed permission paths, checking that pilot users reach the intended data and capabilities through permissions inherited from your Adobe organization.
Coordinate the Adobe onboarding handoff, passing on the validated users, context and review boundaries in one record.
deliverables: Approved context pack: terminology and brand guidance
asks: Administrators who can grant access and confirm the pilot users
Approved source material for business terminology and brand guidance
risk: Pilot users who see more or less than intended: we test each agreed permission path before the pilot starts, and you approve the review boundaries.
outcome: Your pilot users reach the intended data and capabilities in Coworker Chat, working from your approved terminology, brand guidance and review boundaries.
